summary: A 1976 recommendation for a host-to-host protocol for a network that would use ARPANET IMPs without change but allow the upper-level protocols to be redone. It is a lightly edited planning document shared with the community.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 714 proposes a different Host-to-Host Protocol for an ARPANET-type network. It allows traffic in both directions on a connection and uses sequence numbers, credits, and retransmission to manage data flow and message loss.

subtitle: A proposed host protocol combining full-duplex connections with sequence-based flow control.

tldr.problem: The ARPANET Host-to-Host Protocol used separate one-way connections and its flow control and recovery mechanisms had limitations.
tldr.mechanism: The proposal uses full-duplex connections, sequence numbers, and a credit window. Acknowledgements can travel with reverse-direction data, and a sender retransmits unacknowledged messages.
tldr.outcome: The memo specifies an alternative for an ARPANET-type network, adapting ideas from an IFIP protocol while reducing per-message overhead.

facts.label: Message timeout before retransmission
facts.value: More than 30 seconds for the left-edge message

today: RFC 714 presents a proposed Host-to-Host Protocol for an ARPANET-type network. The document describes it as a recommendation circulated to the ARPANET community, not as an adopted replacement.

sections.title: Why Consider Another Host Protocol
sections.content:
The memo describes an ARPANET-like network that would retain its IMPs while allowing a new Host-to-Host protocol. It identifies limitations of the existing protocol, including simplex connections, recovery concerns when messages are lost, and separate flow-control traffic.

The proposed design borrows concepts from the IFIP protocol but aims for less overhead on a single network with short delays and ordered message delivery.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC proposes new host-to-host rules while keeping the network's IMPs. Its aim is to address limits in one-way connections and flow control without carrying all of the IFIP protocol's overhead.

sections.title: Connections and Sliding Windows
sections.content:
A connection carries data in both directions. The receiver grants credits that define how many messages the sender may have in flight; sequence numbers mark messages and acknowledgements move the window forward.

When possible, an acknowledgement and new credit travel with data in the reverse direction. If an acknowledgement does not arrive before a timeout, the sender retransmits the message with the same sequence number, allowing the receiver to detect a duplicate.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver grants room for a limited number of messages. As messages arrive, acknowledgements open room for more, and repeated sequence numbers help identify retransmissions.

sections.title: Establishing and Closing Connections
sections.content:
An RFC command identifies the two sockets, an index, a maximum message size, and initial credit. The connection is established when the two hosts exchange matching RFC commands.

Each side sends and receives a CLS command to complete termination. The protocol also defines reset commands to clear uncertain connection state, an interrupt sent on the control connection, and an echo command for testing.
sections.plainLanguage: The hosts exchange matching requests to establish a connection. To close it, both sides send and receive a close command; reset commands handle cases where their records may no longer agree.

sections.title: Message Format and Recovery
sections.content:
Data messages include a connection index, a sequence number, an acknowledgement, and credit information. The sequence number field is four bits, so it cycles through its values; the window may not be larger than eight messages.

The control connection carries commands such as ACK, NACK, RST, RRP, INT, ECO, and ERP. The memo specifies retransmission after certain IMP errors, a timeout, or a NACK.
sections.plainLanguage: Each data message identifies its connection and place in the sequence, and can report what has arrived in the other direction. Control commands support recovery, interruption, reset, and testing.
